claims.text: The starting Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Exposure at 500–600 °C in an O2-rich environment will rapidly oxidize Mg at the alloy surface.
Surface oxidation under these conditions will produce a continuous MgO layer.
The continuous MgO layer will inhibit further oxidation.
Bulk diffusion kinetics at 500–600 °C will suppress or delay intermetallic nucleation and growth.
The relevant bulk precipitates are Mg-based intermetallic compounds.
High oxygen fugacity favors protective MgO-scale formation.
Competition between oxygen ingress and elemental diffusion determines whether corrosion and oxidation resistance are retained.
If intermetallic precipitation dominates, the oxide layer will become discontinuous.
A discontinuous oxide layer associated with dominant intermetallic precipitation will degrade corrosion resistance.
A discontinuous oxide layer associated with dominant intermetallic precipitation will degrade high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the initial state, O2-treated samples will have a continuous, uniform MgO surface layer.
Relative to the initial state, O2-treated samples will have reduced or delayed bulk intermetallic precipitation.
High oxygen fugacity at 500–600 °C defines the service regime in which oxide growth and diffusion kinetics control the evolution.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that dominant intermetallic precipitation should cause a discontinuous oxide layer, but the predicted-outcome and falsification fields identify the same combination—significant intermetallic precipitation plus a discontinuous MgO scale—as a refutation. Thus, the stated falsification result also matches the hypothesis's proposed converse pathway.
